claim: Missense mutations of valosin-containing protein (VCP) cause an autosomal dominant disease known as inclusion body myopathy, Paget disease with frontotemporal dementia (IBMPFD) and other neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Missense mutations of valosin-containing protein (VCP) cause an autosomal dominant disease known as inclusion body myopathy, Paget disease with frontotemporal dementia (IBMPFD) and other neurodegenerative disorders.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about VCP mutations and IBMPFD.

claim: 90% of IBMPFD patients have myopathy.
source: Because 90% of IBMPFD patients have myopathy, we generated an in vivo IBMPFD model in adult Drosophila muscle, which recapitulates disease pathologies.
evidence: This statistic is cited in the abstract and introduction as established clinical knowledge.

claim: Endogenous VCP negatively regulates Mitofusin, which is required for outer mitochondrial membrane fusion.
source: We show that endogenous VCP negatively regulates Mitofusin, which is required for outer mitochondrial membrane fusion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Common VCP disease mutants act as hyperactive alleles with respect to regulation of Mitofusin.
source: We show that common VCP disease mutants act as hyperactive alleles with respect to regulation of Mitofusin.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing enhanced Mfn degradation.

claim: VCP inhibitors suppress mitochondrial defects, muscle tissue damage and cell death associated with IBMPFD models in Drosophila.
source: Importantly, VCP inhibitors suppress mitochondrial defects, muscle tissue damage and cell death associated with IBMPFD models in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data with NMS-873 and ML240.

claim: VCP inhibitors suppress mitochondrial fusion and respiratory defects in IBMPFD patient fibroblasts.
source: These inhibitors also suppress mitochondrial fusion and respiratory defects in IBMPFD patient fibroblasts.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data from patient cells.

claim: VCP disease mutants cause IBMPFD through a gain-of-function mechanism.
source: These results suggest that VCP disease mutants cause IBMPFD through a gain-of-function mechanism, and that VCP inhibitors have therapeutic value.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing hyperactivity of disease mutants.

claim: VCP inhibitors have therapeutic value for IBMPFD.
source: These results suggest that VCP disease mutants cause IBMPFD through a gain-of-function mechanism, and that VCP inhibitors have therapeutic value.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue experiments with VCP inhibitors in both Drosophila and patient cells.

claim: 90% of IBMPFD patients display skeletal muscle weakness (myopathy), the primary and earliest symptom of IBMPFD.
source: 90% of IBMPFD patients display skeletal muscle weakness (myopathy), the primary and earliest symptom of IBMPFD (Weihl et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Weihl et al., 2009).

claim: 50% of IBMPFD patients will develop Paget's disease of bone, affecting the skull, spine, hips and long bones of all four limbs.
source: With progression of the disease, 50% of patients will develop Paget's disease of bone, affecting the skull, spine, hips and long bones of all four limbs.
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Weihl et al., 2009; Kimonis et al., 2008b).

claim: One-third of IBMPFD patients will develop frontotemporal dementia.
source: One-third of the patients will also develop frontotemporal dementia (Weihl et al., 2009; Kimonis et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Single missense mutations of p97/cdc48/Valosin-containing protein (VCP) cause fully penetrant IBMPFD.
source: Single missense mutations of p97/cdc48/Valosin-containing protein (VCP) cause fully penetrant IBMPFD (Watts et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Watts et al., 2004).

claim: VCP mutations are associated with 1–2% of cases of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), familial hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) and Charcot-Marie-Tooth 2 (CMT2) disease.
source: VCP mutations are also associated with 1–2% of cases of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), familial hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) and Charcot-Marie-Tooth 2 (CMT2) disease (Abramzon et al., 2012; de Bot et al., 2012; Gonzalez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Human p97/VCP and its Drosophila homologue have 85% identity and 93% similarity in protein sequence.
source: Human p97/VCP and its Drosophila homologue have 85% identity and 93% similarity in protein sequence.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about sequence conservation.

claim: VCP has three major domains: the regulatory N domain, and the D1 and D2 ATPase domains.
source: VCP has three major domains: the regulatory N domain, and the D1 and D2 ATPase domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VCP protein structure.

claim: VCP hexameric rings utilize the energy from ATP hydrolysis to promote protein and RNA homeostasis, often by directly or indirectly modifying the fate of ubiquitin-labeled proteins.
source: VCP hexameric rings utilize the energy from ATP hydrolysis to promote protein and RNA homeostasis, often by directly or indirectly modifying the fate of ubiquitin-labeled proteins (Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Meyer et al., 2012).

claim: Disease-causing, single missense mutations of VCP are mainly located in the N-terminal half of the protein, either in the N domain or the D1 domain.
source: Disease-causing, single missense mutations of VCP are mainly located in the N-terminal half of the protein, either in the N domain or the D1 domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the location of disease mutations.

claim: The R155H mutation is the most frequently identified in IBMPFD patients.
source: Among them, the R155H mutation is the most frequently identified in IBMPFD patients, while the A232E mutation is associated with the most severe clinical manifestation (Kimonis et al., 2008a; Ritson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: The A232E mutation is associated with the most severe clinical manifestation of IBMPFD.
source: Among them, the R155H mutation is the most frequently identified in IBMPFD patients, while the A232E mutation is associated with the most severe clinical manifestation (Kimonis et al., 2008a; Ritson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: In vitro assays show that disease mutants have enhanced ATPase activity.
source: In vitro assays show that disease mutants have enhanced ATPase activity (Weihl et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2015; Niwa et al., 2012; Manno et al., 2010; Tang and Xia, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from multiple published studies.

claim: Mitochondrial functional defects, including mitochondrial uncoupling and decreased ATP production, are observed in IBMPFD patient fibroblasts.
source: Mitochondria provide the bulk of the ATP to these tissues through oxidative phosphorylation, and mitochondrial functional defects, including mitochondrial uncoupling and decreased ATP production, are observed in IBMPFD patient fibroblasts (Bartolome et al., 2013; Nalbandian et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Abnormal mitochondria are observed in transgenic VCP disease mutant R155H mice as well as VCP R155H knock-in mice.
source: Abnormal mitochondria are also observed in transgenic VCP disease mutant R155H mice as well as VCP R155H knock-in mice (Custer et al., 2010; Nalbandian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Mitochondrial morphology is controlled by dynamic cycles of fusion, controlled by Mitofusin (Mfn), and fission, regulated by DRP1.
source: Mitochondrial morphology is controlled by dynamic cycles of fusion, controlled by Mitofusin (Mfn), and fission, regulated by DRP1 (Chan, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Chan, 2012).

claim: In mammals, homologous proteins Mitofusin 1 and 2 (Mfn1 and Mfn2) mediate mitochondrial outer membrane fusion.
source: In mammals, homologous proteins Mitofusin 1 and 2 (Mfn1 and Mfn2) mediate mitochondrial outer membrane fusion, with loss of function of Mfn 1 and 2 resulting in fragmented mitochondria and multiple defects in mitochondrial function (Chen et al., 2003b).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Loss of function of Mfn 1 and 2 results in fragmented mitochondria and multiple defects in mitochondrial function.
source: In mammals, homologous proteins Mitofusin 1 and 2 (Mfn1 and Mfn2) mediate mitochondrial outer membrane fusion, with loss of function of Mfn 1 and 2 resulting in fragmented mitochondria and multiple defects in mitochondrial function (Chen et al., 2003b).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: In Hela cells, VCP promotes Mfn 1 degradation.
source: In Hela cells, VCP promotes Mfn 1 degradation (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Xu et al., 2011).

claim: VCP mediates Mfn 1 and 2 degradation when mitophagy is stimulated in mammalian cells.
source: VCP also mediates Mfn 1 and 2 degradation when mitophagy is stimulated in mammalian cells, and overexpression of VCP in Drosophila leads to downregulation of a tagged Mfn-transgene (Kim et al., 2013; Kimura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Overexpression of VCP in Drosophila leads to downregulation of a tagged Mfn-transgene.
source: VCP also mediates Mfn 1 and 2 degradation when mitophagy is stimulated in mammalian cells, and overexpression of VCP in Drosophila leads to downregulation of a tagged Mfn-transgene (Kim et al., 2013; Kimura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Expression of VCP under the control of the pan-muscle Gal4 drivers 24B-Gal4 or Mef2-Gal4 resulted in 100% adult lethality.
source: While expression of VCP under the control of the pan-muscle Gal4 drivers 24B-Gal4 or Mef2-Gal4 resulted in 100% adult lethality, expression of wildtype VCP under IFM control, which provides a pulse of expression in late pupal stages and early adulthood, gave rise to viable flies with intact and healthy muscle following adult eclosion.
evidence: This is an experimental observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: Expression of wildtype VCP under IFM control gave rise to viable flies with intact and healthy muscle following adult eclosion.
source: While expression of VCP under the control of the pan-muscle Gal4 drivers 24B-Gal4 or Mef2-Gal4 resulted in 100% adult lethality, expression of wildtype VCP under IFM control, which provides a pulse of expression in late pupal stages and early adulthood, gave rise to viable flies with intact and healthy muscle following adult eclosion.
evidence: This is an experimental observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: In 2-day-old flies, expression of VCP results in muscle with small mitochondria with intact cristae.
source: In 2-day-old flies, expression of VCP results in muscle with small mitochondria with intact cristae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B').
evidence: This is supported by both text description and electron microscopy images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of UAS-VCP RNAi under IFM control results in mitochondria with an elongated phenotype.
source: Conversely, expression of UAS-VCP RNAi under IFM control (VCP RNAi flies) results in mitochondria with an elongated phenotype (Figure 1C–C'', Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and C').
evidence: This is supported by both text description and microscopy images in Figure 1.

claim: Two independent VCP RNAi lines showed significant knockdown of VCP.
source: Two independent VCP RNAi lines were utilized and both showed significant knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: In homozygous vcp loss-of-function mutants, mitochondria are more tubular and clumped.
source: In contrast, in homozygous vcp loss-of-function mutants mitochondria are more tubular and clumped (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1H and I.

claim: Nurse cells homozygous for a vcp loss-of-function mutant have greatly increased Mfn levels compared to wildtype and heterozygous vcp loss-of-function cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1J–J'', nurse cells homozygous for a vcp loss-of-function mutant have greatly increased Mfn levels compared to wildtype and heterozygous vcp loss-of-function cells.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1J–J''.

claim: Overexpression of wildtype VCP in the flight muscle resulted in a decrease in endogenous Mfn levels.
source: Overexpression of wildtype VCP (VCP OE) in the flight muscle resulted in a decrease in endogenous Mfn levels (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 2A.

claim: VCP overexpression caused a decrease in the levels of Mfn when Mfn was overexpressed using the IFM promoter.
source: VCP overexpression also caused a decrease in the levels of Mfn when Mfn was overexpressed (Mfn OE) using the IFM promoter, suggesting that VCP regulates Mfn post transcriptionally (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 2A and suggests post-transcriptional regulation.

claim: VCP RNAi resulted in an increase in endogenous Mfn levels in a wildtype background.
source: Conversely, VCP RNAi resulted in an increase in endogenous Mfn levels in a wildtype background, and an increase in total Mfn levels in the presence of Mfn OE (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 2B.

claim: VCP overexpression does not alter the levels of pro-fission protein DRP1.
source: In contrast, VCP overexpression does not alter the levels of pro-fission protein DRP1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 2C.

claim: VCP overexpression does not alter the levels of other mitochondrial proteins, such as the outer membrane protein Porin, the inner membrane protein NDUSF3, and the matrix protein MnSOD.
source: In addition, VCP's regulation of Mfn is specific and not part of a general mitophagy response since the levels of other mitochondrial proteins, such as the outer membrane protein Porin, the inner membrane protein NDUSF3, and the matrix protein MnSOD, are not altered (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 2D and suggests specificity of VCP action on Mfn.

claim: Full length VCP strongly interacts with Mfn.
source: Indeed, full length VCP strongly interacts with Mfn (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2E.

claim: VCP interacts with substrate through the D1 ATPase domain, with the presence of the N domain being essential for the interaction.
source: VCP has been shown to interact with substrate through the D1 ATPase domain, with the presence of the N domain being essential for the interaction (Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Meyer et al., 2012).

claim: When the N domain of VCP is deleted, the strength of VCP-Mfn interaction is decreased.
source: As shown in Figure 2E , this is also the case with the VCP-Mfn interaction. When the N domain of VCP is deleted, the strength of VCP-Mfn interaction is decreased, and it is undetectable when N and D1 are both deleted.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2E.

claim: VCP-Mfn interaction is undetectable when N and D1 domains are both deleted.
source: When the N domain of VCP is deleted, the strength of VCP-Mfn interaction is decreased, and it is undetectable when N and D1 are both deleted.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2E.

claim: Removal of the D2 domain has no effect on interaction between VCP and Mfn.
source: In contrast, removal of the D2 domain has no effect on interaction between VCP and Mfn.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2E.

claim: Mfn levels in the input blot are decreased under conditions when VCP and Mfn interact, but not under conditions in which interactions are not observed.
source: Interestingly, Mfn levels in the input blot are decreased under conditions when VCP and Mfn interact, but not under conditions in which interactions are not observed, consistent with the hypothesis that direct interaction between VCP and Mfn is required for Mfn degradation.
evidence: This is an observation from the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2E that supports the hypothesis of direct interaction-dependent degradation.

claim: Direct interaction between VCP and Mfn is required for Mfn degradation.
source: Interestingly, Mfn levels in the input blot are decreased under conditions when VCP and Mfn interact, but not under conditions in which interactions are not observed, consistent with the hypothesis that direct interaction between VCP and Mfn is required for Mfn degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between VCP-Mfn interaction and Mfn degradation observed in Figure 2E.

claim: Mfn is a specific, direct target of VCP.
source: Together, these observations suggest that Mfn is a specific, direct target of VCP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the physical interaction data and specificity of regulation.

claim: PINK1 and Parkin function in the same pathway, with PINK1 positively regulating Parkin to control mitochondrial integrity and quality control in Drosophila.
source: We and others have shown that PINK1 and Parkin function in the same pathway, with PINK1 positively regulating Parkin to control mitochondrial integrity and quality control in Drosophila (Clark et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2006; Park et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from published literature including the authors' own work.

claim: Levels of Mfn are significantly increased in PINK1 and parkin null mutants.
source: Importantly, levels of Mfn are significantly increased in PINK1 and parkin null mutants and downregulation of Mfn protein levels suppresses phenotypes in both mutants (Deng et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2008; Park et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Downregulation of Mfn protein levels suppresses phenotypes in PINK1 and parkin null mutants.
source: Importantly, levels of Mfn are significantly increased in PINK1 and parkin null mutants and downregulation of Mfn protein levels suppresses phenotypes in both mutants (Deng et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2008; Park et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Expression of VCP completely suppressed tissue damage and mitochondrial defects in PINK1 and parkin null mutants.
source: VCP OE completely suppressed tissue damage and mitochondrial defects (Figure 3C–C''' and E–E''').
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 3.

claim: The thorax indentation phenotype in PINK1/parkin mutants is completely suppressed by VCP overexpression under the control of the IFM-Gal4 driver, but not the EDTP-Gal4 driver.
source: The thorax indentation phenotype in PINK1/parkin mutants is also completely suppressed by VCP overexpression under the control of the IFM-Gal4 driver, but not the EDTP-Gal4 driver (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: VCP OE significantly reduced the accumulation of Mfn normally observed in both PINK1 and parkin mutants.
source: As predicted for a mechanism of VCP action that occurs through regulation of Mfn, VCP OE significantly reduced the accumulation of Mfn normally observed in both mutants (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 3F.

claim: Expression of VCP resulted in a dramatic rescue of mitochondrial morphology due to lack of both parkin and mul1.
source: Remarkably, expression of VCP resulted in a dramatic rescue of mitochondrial morphology due to lack of both parkin and mul1 (Figure 3G–I').
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 3G–I'.

claim: VCP-dependent suppression of PINK1 null, parkin null and parkin mul1 double phenotypes occurs through downregulaton of Mfn levels.
source: Together, these results suggest that VCP-dependent suppression of PINK1 null, parkin null and parkin mul1 double phenotypes occurs through downregulaton of Mfn levels (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments and Mfn level measurements.

claim: VCP regulates Mfn levels under non-stress conditions.
source: Together, our observations argue that VCP regulates Mfn levels under non-stress conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations in non-stressed cells.

claim: VCP-dependent regulation of Mfn does not require PINK1 or Parkin.
source: They also show that VCP-dependent regulation of Mfn does not require PINK1 or parkin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ability of VCP to suppress PINK1 and parkin mutant phenotypes.

claim: Pathologies observed in IBMPFD patient muscle include muscle cell death, changes in mitochondrial morphology, damaged tissue integrity, TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP43) mislocalization to the cytosol, and formation of autophagic marker p62 and ubiquitin aggregates.
source: The pathologies observed in IBMPFD patient muscle, and in muscle from VCP disease mutant transgenic and mouse knock-in models, include muscle cell death, changes in mitochondrial morphology, damaged tissue integrity, TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP43) mislocalization to the cytosol, and formation of autophagic marker p62 and ubiquitin aggregates, signs of multisystem proteinopathy (Ju et al., 2009; Ritson et al., 2010; Nalbandian et al., 2012; Ritz et al., 2011; Nalbandian et al., 2015b; Weihl, 2011; Ahmed et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from multiple published studies.

claim: VCP WT, VCP RH and VCP AE are expressed at comparable level in the fly's thorax.
source: Anti-VCP antibody blotting shows that VCP WT, VCP RH and VCP AE are expressed at comparable level in the fly's thorax (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4B.

claim: Muscle from flies expressing VCP RH or VCP AE showed extensive cell death (97 ± 3.6% and 95.7 ± 5.1% muscle are TUNEL-positive).
source: In contrast, muscle from flies expressing VCP RH or VCP AE under IFM-Gal4 control (thereafter called VCP RH or VCP AE flies) showed extensive cell death (97 ± 3.6% and 95.7 ± 5.1% muscle are TUNEL-positive), defective MitoGFP signals (Figure 4D'' and D'''), and severely disrupted muscle integrity (Figure 4E'' and E''').
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 4D'' and D'''.

claim: IFMs from VCP RH and AE flies showed a decrease in the intensity of the nuclear TDP43 signal, and an increase in the intensity of staining associated with puncta in the sarcoplasmic area.
source: In addition, while in wildtype and VCP WT flies TDP43 was found in IFM nuclear and sarcoplasmic compartments, IFMs from VCP RH and AE flies showed a decrease in the intensity of the nuclear signal, and an increase in the intensity of staining associated with puncta in the sarcoplasmic area (Figure 4C,F–F''').
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4F–F'''.

claim: Muscle from VCP RH and AE flies contained large aggregates of anti-p62 and anti-ubiquitin staining.
source: Muscle from VCP RH and AE flies also contained large aggregates of anti-p62 and anti-ubiquitin staining. These were not observed in wildtype or VCP WT flies (Figure 4G–H''').
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4G–H'''.

claim: The pathologies observed in flight muscle at day 6 post eclosion were not present at day 2.
source: Importantly, the pathologies observed in flight muscle at day 6 post eclosion were not present at day 2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting the degenerative nature of the pathology, as with the human disease and mouse models (Kimonis et al., 2008a; Custer et al., 2010; Nalbandian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and suggests progressive degeneration.

claim: IFM-specific expression of VCP RH and AE recapitulates a broad spectrum of IBMPFD disease pathologies.
source: Together, these observations indicate that IFM-specific expression of VCP RH and AE recapitulates a broad spectrum of IBMPFD disease pathologies and forms the strong basis for further investigation of disease mechanisms and treatment studies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multiple pathological features observed in the Drosophila model.

claim: In VCP RH and AE muscle, mitochondria are smaller in size, and more fragmented than in VCP WT flies.
source: In VCP RH and AE muscle, however, mitochondria are smaller in size, and more fragmented than in VCP WT flies. In addition, they also have severe ultrastructural defects under EM studies with a broken cristae (Figure 5C–D').
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 5C–D'.

claim: VCP RH and AE mitochondria have severe ultrastructural defects with broken cristae.
source: In VCP RH and AE muscle, however, mitochondria are smaller in size, and more fragmented than in VCP WT flies. In addition, they also have severe ultrastructural defects under EM studies with a broken cristae (Figure 5C–D').
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 5C–D'.

claim: Expression of VCP RH and AE leads to a further reduction in Mfn as compared to VCP WT.
source: Expression of VCP RH and AE lead to a further reduction in Mfn as compared to VCP WT.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5F.

claim: Expression of VCP ATPase defective mutant E2Q does not significantly change the Mfn level in fly thoraxes.
source: Expression of VCP ATPase defective mutant E2Q (p=0.097, independent t test, N = 3) does not significantly change the Mfn level in fly thoraxes as compared with Gal4 control.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5F.

claim: VCP RH and AE are hyperactive alleles with respect to promoting downregulation of Mfn levels.
source: These results suggest that VCP disease mutants are hyperactive with respect to promoting downregulation of Mfn levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the greater reduction in Mfn levels by disease mutants compared to WT VCP.

claim: Expression of VCP RH and AE mutants, but not VCP E2Q or VCP RNAi, robustly restored mitochondrial structure in the parkin null mutant.
source: As shown in Figure 5G–J, expression of VCP RH and AE mutants, but not VCP E2Q or VCP RNAi, robustly restored mitochondrial structure, as indicated by MitoGFP fluorescence, in the parkin null mutant (Figure 5K and L).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 5G–L.

claim: The accumulation of Mfn in parkin mutants was significantly reduced in the presence of VCP WT, RH and AE, with VCP RH and AE causing greater decreases in Mfn levels than VCP WT.
source: Moreover, corresponding to the mitochondrial phenotypes, the accumulation of Mfn in parkin mutants was significantly reduced in the presence of VCP WT, RH and AE, with VCP RH and AE causing greater decreases in Mfn levels than VCP WT (Figure 5S).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 5S.

claim: VCP RH and AE expression robustly rescued the mitochondrial defects in the parkin mul1 double null mutants, but expression of VCP E2Q or VCP RNAi did not.
source: In addition, VCP RH and AE expression also robustly rescued the mitochondrial defects in the parkin mul1 double null mutants, but an expression of VCP E2Q or VCP RNAi did not (Figure 5M–R).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 5M–R.

claim: VCP RH and AE disease mutants do not behave as ATPase defective or loss-of-function mutants, and instead are hyperactive with respect to regulation of Mfn.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that VCP RH and AE disease mutants do not behave as ATPase defective or loss-of-function mutants, and instead are hyperactive with respect to regulation of Mfn.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments and Mfn level measurements.

claim: mfn muscle-specific knockdown flies have fragmented mitochondria, TDP43 mislocalization, vacuole formation, p62 and ubiquitin accumulation.
source: Indeed, mfn muscle-specific knockdown flies have fragmented mitochondria (Figure 4I–I'), TDP43 mislocalization (Figure 4J–J'), vacuole formation (Figure 4K–K'), p62 and ubiquitin accumulation (Figure 4L–L' and M–M'), as with the VCP disease mutants.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 4I–M'.

claim: Addition of 2 copies of an mfn genomic rescue transgene resulted in a suppression of the mitochondrial fragmentation and cristae phenotypes in 2-day-old VCP RH and AE flies.
source: We were, however, able to bring about a mild increase in Mfn levels through addition of 2 copies of an mfn genomic rescue transgene in the background of VCP RH and AE expressing flies. Interestingly, this resulted in a suppression of the mitochondrial fragmentation and cristae phenotypes in 2-day-old VCP RH and AE flies (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) but not the pathology observed in VCP RH and AE fly muscles at 6 days (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Downregulation of Mfn is an important contributor to IBMPFD muscle pathology.
source: Together, our data suggest that downregulation of Mfn is an important contributor to IBMPFD muscle pathology.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phenotypic similarities between mfn knockdown and VCP disease mutant expression.

claim: The basal level Oxygen Consumption Rate (OCR) in the VCP RH patient cells is slightly decreased compared to the healthy control.
source: As shown in Figure 6A, the basal level Oxygen Consumption Rate (OCR) in the VCP RH patient cells is slightly decreased compared to the healthy control, suggesting that baseline mitochondrial respiratory chain function is compromised in patient cells.
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse assay data in Figure 6A.

claim: Maximum OCR, measured in the presence of the uncoupler FCCP, is significantly decreased in VCP RH IBMPFD patient cells.
source: Maximum OCR, measured in the presence of the uncoupler FCCP, is significantly decreased in VCP RH IBMPFD patient cells.
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse assay data in Figure 6A.

claim: The spare OCR in IBMPFD patient cells is significantly decreased as compared with controls.
source: The spare OCR, which is calculated by subtracting the basal OCR from the maximum OCR, provides a measure of reserve mitochondrial capacity for ATP generation. The spare OCR in IBMPFD patient cells is significantly decreased as compared with controls.
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse assay data in Figure 6A.

claim: Mfn 1 and 2 levels in VCP RH cells were reduced to 0.66 ± 0.14 and 0.60 ± 0.14 respectively, as compared with age and gender matched healthy control cells.
source: Mfn 1 and 2 levels in VCP RH cells were reduced to 0.66 ± 0.14 and 0.60 ± 0.14 respectively, as compared with age and gender matched healthy control cells (set as 1, Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 6B.

claim: In the VCP RH IBMPFD patient cells, the GFP signal decrease after photoactivation is significantly delayed compared to control cells.
source: In control cells, PA-GFP gradually decreases after photoactivation; in the VCP RH IBMPFD patient cells, the GFP signal decrease is significantly delayed (Figure 6C–D', E).
evidence: This is supported by mitochondrial fusion assay data in Figure 6C–E.

claim: The VCP RH mutation results in a decrease in Mfn 1 and 2 levels that lead to impaired mitochondrial fusion.
source: These data suggest that the VCP RH mutation results in a decrease in Mfn 1 and 2 levels that lead to impaired mitochondrial fusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Mfn level measurements and fusion assay results.

claim: The VCP mutant impairs both basal and maximal mitochondrial respiratory function.
source: In addition, the VCP mutant impairs both basal and maximal mitochondrial respiratory function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the OCR measurements in patient cells.

claim: NMS-873 is a highly specific and robust VCP ATPase inhibitor.
source: NMS-873, 3-[3-Cyclopentylsulfanyl-5-(4'-methanesulfonyl-2-methyl-biphenyl-4-yloxymethyl)-[1, 2, 4] triazol-4-yl]-pyridine, an allosteric inhibitor of VCP ATPase activity, is a highly specific and robust VCP ATPase inhibitor (Magnaghi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Magnaghi et al., 2013).

claim: ML240 competitively blocks ATP binding to VCP.
source: ML240, 2-(2-Amino-1H-benzimidazol-1-yl)−8-methoxy-N-(phenylmethyl)−4-quinazolinamine is another potent inhibitor, which competitively blocks ATP binding to VCP (Chou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Chou et al., 2013).

claim: NMS-873 or ML240 feeding resulted in dramatic mitochondrial elongation in wildtype animals.
source: NMS-873 or ML240 feeding resulted in dramatic mitochondrial elongation in wildtype animals as visualized with MitoGFP using light microscopy (Figure 7A–A'') and at the ultrastructural level using EM (Figure 7B–B''').
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 7A–B'''.

claim: The smaller mitochondria phenotype associated with overexpression of VCP WT was significantly suppressed following feeding with 30 µM NMS-873 or 30 µM ML240.
source: The smaller mitochondria phenotype associated with overexpression of VCP WT was also significantly suppressed following feeding with 30 µM NMS-873 or 30 µM ML240 (Figure 7C–C''').
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 7C–C'''.

claim: Feeding with NMS-873 and ML240 reversed the phenotypic rescue of mitochondrial defects caused by expression of VCP WT, RH and AE in PINK1 mutants.
source: Feeding with NMS-873 and ML240 also reversed the phenotypic rescue of mitochondrial defects caused by expression of VCP WT, RH and AE in PINK1 mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Feeding with NMS-873 resulted in a dose-dependent increase in the levels of Mfn.
source: Supporting these results, feeding with NMS-873 also resulted in a dose-dependent increase in the levels of Mfn (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 7D.

claim: NMS-873 and ML240 inhibit endogenous VCP in vivo, resulting in a phenocopy of loss of VCP function.
source: Together, these observations suggest that NMS-873 and ML240 inhibit endogenous VCP in vivo, resulting in a phenocopy of loss of VCP function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mitochondrial elongation and Mfn accumulation observed with inhibitor treatment.

claim: NMS-873 and ML240 feeding largely prevented muscle cell death caused by expression of VCP RH or AE.
source: Strikingly, NMS-873 and ML240 feeding largely prevented muscle cell death caused by expression of VCP RH or AE (Figure 8A–B'').
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 8A–B''.

claim: NMS-873 and ML240 feeding significantly rescued disrupted muscle integrity in VCP RH and AE flies.
source: It also significantly rescued disrupted muscle integrity (Figure 8C–D'').
evidence: This is supported by Toluidine Blue staining data in Figure 8C–D''.

claim: NMS-873 and ML240 feeding rescued mitochondrial size, cristae structure, and myofibril organization at the ultrastructural level in VCP RH and AE flies.
source: Rescue of mitochondrial size, cristae structure, and myofibril organization was also observed at the ultrastructural level (Figure 8E–F'').
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 8E–F''.

claim: VCP inhibitor feeding resulted in significant rescue of phenotypes associated with p62, ubiquitin and TDP43 in VCP RH and AE expressing flies.
source: Finally, we note that VCP inhibitor feeding also resulted in significant rescue of a number of other phenotypes in VCP RH and AE expressing flies, including those associated with p62, ubiquitin and TDP43 (Figure 8G–L'').
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 8G–L''.

claim: VCP disease mutants are hyperactive in multiple aspects, and disease phenotypes can be suppressed by inhibition of VCP ATPase activity.
source: Together, these observations suggest that VCP disease mutants are hyperactive in multiple aspects, and that disease phenotypes can be suppressed by inhibition of VCP ATPase activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments with VCP inhibitors.

claim: Treatment with 250 nM ML240 for 6 hr increased Mfn 1 levels in immortalized IBMPFD patient fibroblasts.
source: As shown in Figure 9A, immortalized IBMPFD patient fibroblasts have decreased Mfn 1 levels, and these are increased by treatment with 250 nM ML240 for 6 hr.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 9A.

claim: Mitochondrial fusion defects in IBMPFD patient fibroblasts were significantly rescued after 6 hr of treatment with 250 nM ML240.
source: However, in a more sensitive assay in which rates of fusion are measured directly, mitochondrial fusion defects in IBMPFD patient fibroblasts were significantly rescued after 6 hr of treatment with 250 nM ML240 (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by mitochondrial fusion assay data in Figure 9B.

claim: 50 nM and 100 nM ML240 treatment for 4 days significantly enhanced the basal and maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) in patient fibroblasts.
source: Finally, 50 nM and 100 nM ML240 treatment for 4 days also significantly enhanced the basal and maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) in patient fibroblasts (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse assay data in Figure 9C.

claim: 1 nM and 10 nM NMS-873 treatment for 6 days significantly enhanced the maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) in patient fibroblasts.
source: Similarly, 1 nM and 10 nM NMS-873 treatment for 6 days significantly enhanced the maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) in patient fibroblasts as well (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse assay data in Figure 9D.

claim: Two inhibitors with different mechanisms generate similar results in terms of rescuing IBMFPD pathologies, reducing the likelihood that these are off-targeting effects.
source: The fact that two inhibitors with different mechanisms generate similar results in terms of rescuing IBMFPD pathologies reduces the likelihood that these are off-targeting effects.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the consistency of results with two different inhibitors.

claim: VCP inhibitors have potential as therapeutic tools for IBMPFD disease.
source: Together, these data strongly support the effects of VCP inhibitors as potential therapeutic tools for IBMPFD disease.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments in both Drosophila and patient cells.

claim: Endogenous VCP regulates mitochondrial fusion.
source: Endogenous VCP regulates mitochondrial fusion (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is a summary statement of a primary finding, supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Loss of VCP function leads to increased Mfn levels and increased mitochondrial size in multiple tissues.
source: Loss of VCP function leads to increased Mfn levels and increased mitochondrial size in multiple tissues.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from VCP RNAi and loss-of-function mutant experiments.

claim: VCP overexpression results in reduced Mfn levels and decreased mitochondrial size.
source: Conversely, VCP overexpression results in reduced Mfn levels and decreased mitochondrial size.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from VCP overexpression experiments.

claim: VCP physically interacts with Mfn via domains that are also used to bind its substrates in other contexts.
source: VCP physically interacts with Mfn via domains that are also used to bind its substrates in other contexts.
evidence: This is a summary of the co-immunoprecipitation findings.

claim: Mfn is likely an endogenous VCP substrate.
source: Thus, it is likely that Mfn is an endogenous VCP substrate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the physical interaction and regulation data.

claim: VCP-dependent removal of Mfn does not require Parkin or Mul1, E3 ligases known to ubiquitinate Mfn.
source: We show that VCP-dependent removal of Mfn does not require Parkin or Mul1, E3 ligases known to ubiquitinate Mfn.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments in parkin and mul1 mutants.

claim: Expression of VCP disease mutants results in tissue damage, mitochondrial fusion defects and decreased levels of Mfn compared to VCP WT.
source: We show that compared to VCP WT, expression of VCP disease mutants results in tissue damage, mitochondrial fusion defects and decreased levels of Mfn (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from the Drosophila disease model.

claim: VCP disease mutants do not function as loss-of-function or dominant negative mutants, but rather as dominant activated mutants in regulating Mfn levels and bringing about mitochondrial fusion defects.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that VCP disease mutants do not function as loss-of-function or dominant negative mutants, but rather as dominant activated mutants in regulating Mfn levels and bringing about mitochondrial fusion defects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of disease mutants with WT and ATPase-defective mutants.

claim: Mitochondrial fusion and Mfn levels are decreased in VCP disease mutant fibroblasts.
source: This conclusion is further supported by our findings that mitochondrial fusion and Mfn levels are also decreased in VCP disease mutant fibroblasts.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from patient fibroblast studies.

claim: VCP overexpression suppresses a parkin null mutant in addition to a PINK1 null.
source: Our finding that VCP overexpression suppresses a parkin null mutant in addition to a PINK1 null stands in contrast to what was reported in Kim et al., who proposed that VCP-dependent degradation of Mfn required recruitment by Parkin.
evidence: This is an experimental finding that contrasts with previous literature.

claim: VCP overexpression suppresses phenotypes due to double mutants of parkin and mul1.
source: In addition, we also find that VCP overexpression suppresses phenotypes due to double mutants of parkin and mul1, which acts in a parallel pathway to degrade Mfn (Yun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: VCP-dependent regulation of Mfn does not require PINK1 or parkin under non-stress conditions.
source: Together, these observations show that VCP-dependent regulation of Mfn does not require PINK1 or parkin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments.

claim: Parkin activation may further promote VCP-dependent Mfn degradation under some conditions.
source: However, these results do not exclude models in which Parkin activation further promotes VCP-dependent Mfn degradation, which may or may not involve mitophagy, under some conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging alternative models.

claim: In vitro biochemistry studies suggest that VCP disease mutants have increased ATPase activities, favoring a dominant active model.
source: Regarding the mechanisms of VCP disease mutant action, in vitro biochemistry studies suggest that they have increased ATPase activities, thus favoring a dominant active model (Weihl et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2015; Niwa et al., 2012; Manno et al., 2010; Tang and Xia, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: In vivo data from Drosophila shows that eye phenotypes caused by VCP disease mutant expression can be alleviated through loss of one copy of wildtype VCP.
source: In addition, in vivo data from Drosophila shows that eye phenotypes caused by VCP disease mutant expression can be alleviated through loss of one copy of wildtype VCP. This also is consistent with models in which VCP mutants have increased activity (Chang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Chang et al., 2011).

claim: VCP disease mutant expression led to mitochondria respiratory chain defects, as did VCP RNAi.
source: In contrast, in cell culture studies Bartolome, et al showed that VCP disease mutant expression led to mitochondria respiratory chain defects, as did VCP RNAi (Bartolome et al., 2013);
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Bartolome et al., 2013).

claim: VCP disease mutant expression impaired endocytosis to the same extent as that of VCP ATPase defective mutants.
source: Ritz, et al showed that VCP disease mutant expression impaired endocytosis to the same extent as that of VCP ATPase defective mutants (Ritz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from published literature (Ritz et al., 2011).

claim: Either an increase or a decrease in the levels of VCP activity can lead to mitochondrial defects.
source: For example, an alternative interpretation of the impairment of respiratory chain function observed following VCP disease mutant expression or following VCP RNAi is that either an increase or a decrease in the levels of VCP activity leads to mitochondrial defects, which is what we observed in this study.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: VCP inhibitors potently rescue multiple VCP disease phenotypes in flies and patient cells.
source: Indeed, we find VCP inhibitors potently rescue multiple VCP disease phenotypes in flies and patient cells (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings with VCP inhibitors.

claim: Suppression by VCP inhibitors includes phenotypes beyond mitochondria, involving TDP43, p62 and ubiquitin.
source: Importantly, suppression includes phenotypes beyond mitochondria (Figure 10C), involving TDP43, p62 and ubiquitin, suggesting that these inhibitors are likely to be effective in therapeutic settings.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings and a conclusion about therapeutic potential.

claim: Drosophila fed inhibitors are suppressed with respect to VCP disease phenotypes, but otherwise develop normally.
source: Our observation that Drosophila fed inhibitors are suppressed with respect to VCP disease phenotypes, but otherwise develop normally, suggests that this therapeutic goal may be possible.
evidence: This is an experimental observation that supports the feasibility of therapeutic use.

claim: VCP disease mutants are associated with sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, hereditary spastic paraplegia and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.
source: Finally, VCP disease mutants are associated with sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Abramzon et al., 2012), and hereditary spastic paraplegia (de Bot et al., 2012) and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (Gonzalez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: VCP inhibitors may have therapeutic value for sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, hereditary spastic paraplegia and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.
source: Our findings suggest possible therapeutic values of VCP inhibitors for these diseases.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the association of VCP mutations with these diseases and the efficacy of inhibitors in IBMPFD models.
